questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: What a headline puts in the foreground
questions.learningObjective: identify what a French headline promotes to the first line
questions.stem: A news site's headline reads: « La mairie suspend le projet pour la troisième fois en deux ans » What has the headline chosen to put in front?

options.text: The number of suspensions and the length of the period, with the reasons left to the article
The name of the mayor, which the headline has deliberately kept out of the line
options.misconception: reads an omission as a suppression and expects a name that a headline need not carry

options.text: The cost of the project, which the reader can work out from the single verb suspendre
options.misconception: believes a headline supplies the consequences and leaves the article to work them out

options.text: The opinion of the paper, which a French headline never states in the first line
options.misconception: expects a headline to carry the paper's opinion, which French headlines leave to the text

questions.explanation: A French headline promotes the fact a reader compares while scanning, and holds back everything that would need a subordinate clause. The number of suspensions and the span of two years are the news, because both are countable and both are what makes the story a pattern. The reasons, the cost and the mayor's name can all wait for the article. The trap is expecting a whole story in one line, and then reading the missing parts as though they had been suppressed.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the line a reader could repeat while scanning a page.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Reading the audience of an advertisement
questions.learningObjective: infer the addressee from the restrictions an advert carries
questions.stem: An advertisement reads: « Moins de 30 000 francs par mois, sans engagement, pour les étudiants de moins de 26 ans. » Who is this addressed to?

options.text: To people under 26 with little money and no wish to be tied down, as all three details show
To everybody at once, since the price is the only fact stated and nothing narrows the offer
options.misconception: reads a price as a universal offer and misses the two restrictions printed beside it

options.text: To employers, because a monthly figure is the unit a company budget is written in
options.misconception: treats a sum in francs as a business figure and hands it to a buyer rather than a payer

options.text: To retired readers, since a sum below thirty thousand is roughly what a pension comes to
options.misconception: takes a low figure as a pension-level amount and ignores the stated age limit

questions.explanation: The audience of a French advert can be read off its restrictions as easily as off its claims. « Moins de 26 ans » sets a limit, « sans engagement » sets a wish, and « moins de 30 000 francs par mois » sets a budget; all three describe one person rather than a market. A price alone describes everybody. The trap is treating the figure as the message and the restrictions as fine print, when the restrictions are what turn a number into an offer for a particular reader.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader would have to be like for all three conditions to fit at once.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: What a character limit does to a post
questions.learningObjective: say what a length constraint pushes out of a claim
questions.stem: A social post must fit one character limit and one picture. What does that constraint do to the content, and what does it push out?

options.text: It forces one idea per post and squeezes out the qualification, the source and the date
It allows several linked ideas, as long as each one is short enough to fit the box
options.misconception: believes the limit constrains characters but not the number of claims carried inside them

options.text: It removes the need for a source, on the grounds that a short claim needs no support
options.misconception: takes brevity for evidence and mistakes a constraint for a warrant

options.text: It rewards the longest possible sentence, since filling the box is what the format asks for
options.misconception: picks length as the thing the box rewards and so fills it with an argument nobody asked for

questions.explanation: A character limit is an editorial constraint before it is anything else, and it does to a claim what a shop counter does to a bag: everything that will not fit goes. What survives is the assertion itself, and what is lost is the material that would let a reader judge it — the hedge, the date, the place the figure came from. The trap is expecting the format to be neutral. A short post is not a cautious post; it is a post with the cautious parts removed.
questions.hint: Ask which part of a careful claim could not be made to fit.

questions.topic: The disclosure an influencer owes
questions.learningObjective: say what a commercial tag declares and why it is required
questions.stem: A creator posts a picture of a kitchen gadget and adds « (partenariat) » at the end. What does that tag do that a caption without it does not?

options.text: It declares the post as paid, which is the disclosure the creator is obliged to make
It declares the gadget as faulty, and warns other buyers away from the product
options.misconception: reads a disclosure as a confession of fault and reverses the whole sense of the tag

options.text: It declares the post as private, and limits the audience to the creator's followers
options.misconception: confuses a declaration of interest with a control over who is able to see the post

options.text: It declares the creator as new, and dates the account to the present campaign
options.misconception: takes a commercial tag for a statement about the state of the account

questions.explanation: A post that has been paid for has to be marked as paid, and in France the creator's obligation is to make that visible where the audience is looking, not in a list of disclosures at the foot of a page. « Publicité » is the legal word, « partenariat » or « collaboration commerciale » is the ordinary one, and both are read by an audience that has been trained to discount the untagged recommendation. questions.topic: What makes a review worth checking
questions.learningObjective: judge a review by what it makes testable
questions.stem: Two reviews of a restaurant are compared. One reads « Excellent, cinq étoiles », the other reads « Service lent un samedi soir, mais le plat est arrivé chaud et l'addition pour deux était de 38 euros ». Which is worth more as evidence?

options.text: The second, because it names what happened, when, and at what price, and can be checked
The first, because a five-star rating is the summary of many separate visits
options.misconception: reads a rating as an average of many visits when a rating is one person's single judgement

options.text: The first, because a short opinion is far less likely to have been written for money
options.misconception: assumes that brevity proves honesty, which is a claim about length and not about payment

options.text: The second, because only a long review has taken the trouble to visit at all
options.misconception: confuses the ability to check a claim with the effort of writing it, which are not the same

questions.explanation: The test of a review is whether a reader could go and see for themselves what it reports, and the second review passes: a slow service on a Saturday evening, a hot dish, forty euros for two. The first review cannot be checked and cannot be contradicted either, and a rating is a single person's judgement written in the form of a number. The trap is confusing a claim that is easy to check with a claim that took more effort, which is a different virtue and says nothing about truth.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: What sourcing in a report is doing
questions.learningObjective: separate attribution in a report from verification of the claim
questions.stem: A report reads: « Selon l'institut national de la statistique, le chiffre est passé de 4 à 6 %. Le ministère n'a pas commenté à ce jour. » What work is the sourcing doing?

options.text: It names who measured the figure and records that nobody official has answered for it
It makes the figure more authoritative than a ministry statement would have made it
options.misconception: treats a named body as a guarantee and mistakes attribution for verification

options.text: It relieves the paper of checking the figure, since the number came from somewhere else
options.misconception: hands the paper an exemption from checking a figure it has chosen to publish

options.text: It shows the paper is convinced the number is right, which a named source is meant to prove
options.misconception: takes attribution as endorsement and so reports the figure as the paper's own claim

questions.explanation: « Selon » names the body that did the measuring, and the second sentence records the other half of good sourcing: nobody in authority has answered. A report that gives both lets a reader weigh the number, and a report that gives only the comfortable quote cannot be weighed at all. Attribution is not verification, since a named body can be named wrongly or quoted selectively. The trap is reading the source as the paper's own belief and so inheriting it without a check.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could still not know after reading both sentences.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: What a fact-check verifies
questions.learningObjective: keep a fact-check to the one question it answers
questions.stem: A fact-check page gives a verdict of « Faux », then the claim, its date, three sources, and finally a paragraph on how the claim spread. What has it verified?

options.text: That the claim is false on stated evidence, and not why the people who shared it believed it
That the claim is false, why it spread, and that whoever spread it meant to deceive
options.misconception: adds a claim about motive that a fact-check does not establish and could not establish

options.text: That the claim is true in substance, and that only the wording of it is loose
options.misconception: reverses the verdict and then reports the wording as though it were the whole fault

options.text: That no reasonable reader could have told this claim apart from a true one
options.misconception: describes a reader's state of mind rather than the state of the evidence

questions.explanation: A fact-check answers one question, which is whether a claim is supported by the evidence, and the verdict sits at the top with the sources underneath it so that the reader can disagree on the evidence rather than on the tone. The paragraph on circulation is a separate section: it explains how a claim travelled without deciding what anybody meant by it. The trap is expecting one label to do two jobs, and so reading a verdict on the evidence as a verdict on the people who repeated it.
questions.hint: Ask which of the page's four parts a reader could disagree with without the verdict changing.

questions.topic: What a ranking actually optimises for
questions.learningObjective: read a platform's claim about its feed against its own measures
questions.stem: A platform says: « Nous vous montrons ce qui vous intéresse. » What is the ranking actually optimising for?

options.text: For the measures the platform already holds about you, not for your stated interests
For the words you have typed into the search box during the past week
options.misconception: confuses a search box with a feed and assumes the ranking follows a query

options.text: For what most people on the platform prefer, since that is the fairest measure available
options.misconception: assumes a system tuned to a measured signal also ends up at the popular choice

options.text: For what an editor has decided is worth reading, chosen by hand every morning
options.misconception: assumes a hand-picked editorial choice where the ranking is computed from behaviour

questions.explanation: A ranking works from what it has already recorded: what was watched to the end, what was opened twice, what was passed on. Those measures stand in for interest whether or not they match it, and « ce qui vous intéresse » is the platform's word for the substitute rather than for the thing itself. A search box is a request and a feed is not. The trap is the fairness claim, since a system optimised for a measurable signal has no reason to arrive at the popular choice.
questions.hint: Ask what the platform can actually see, and what it asks you about.

questions.topic: The signal a recommendation feed rewards
questions.learningObjective: name the measurable behaviour behind a feed's choices
questions.stem: A feed keeps showing short videos the viewer watched to the end, and has stopped showing longer ones they also liked. What is the feed optimising for?

options.text: For completion, because a video watched to the end is the cheapest signal it can measure
For satisfaction, because liking a video shows the viewer is satisfied with it
options.misconception: treats a cheap measure as if it were the thing the viewer actually wants

options.text: For length, because longer videos carry more advertising and so earn the platform more
options.misconception: supposes the feed is built for the platform's income rather than for a measured signal

options.text: For variety, because a good feed ought to show the viewer something new every time
options.misconception: expects variety from a system that has been asked to maximise one measurable thing

The trap is the wishful version, in which a good feed is expected to introduce the viewer to something new, when the only thing the system was asked to do was to predict one more view.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: How a filter bubble forms
questions.learningObjective: identify the mechanism behind a narrowed news feed
questions.stem: A reader notices that a news app now shows only the arguments they already agree with. Which mechanism produces that?

options.text: Ranking by signals of past agreement, which keeps showing what has already been rewarded
The deliberate choice of an editor to spare readers from difficult opinions
options.misconception: looks for a person where there is only an automated ranking taking the decisions

options.text: A national rule limiting the political content that an app is allowed to carry
options.misconception: invents a legal constraint that no such rule produces and that nobody has cited

options.text: The effect of switching off cookies, which removes the app's memory of the reader
options.misconception: confuses a privacy setting with a filtering mechanism and predicts the opposite of what happens

Every step is a reasonable decision and the result is a reader who never meets the other side. The trap is looking for a person, or a law, at the point where only a measurement is working.
questions.hint: Ask who decided the content on the previous screen, and how they decided it.

questions.learningObjective: say what a tag adds that a caption does not
questions.stem: A post carries the tag #renchef. What does the tag do that the words of the caption do not?

It hides the post from the followers who did not follow the creator in the first place
options.misconception: confuses a discovery label with a restriction on who is able to see the post

options.text: It makes the post official, so that the platform treats it as an advertisement
options.misconception: takes a label as a declaration of official status, which no tag in fact confers

options.text: It shortens the caption, since the words inside a tag do not count towards the limit
options.misconception: believes a tag reduces the amount of text rather than adding to what has to be written

questions.explanation: A hashtag is an index entry. It adds the post to a set that a reader who did not know the creator can browse, and it does this by giving the post a name that matches a word a stranger would search for. The trap is treating the tag as a control or a status, when it is only a label, and a label that is ignored by the platform changes nothing at all.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: What a livestream does to conversation
questions.learningObjective: describe the one-directional stretch of a live chat
questions.stem: During a livestream the chat panel scrolls faster than the streamer can read it. What does that do to the exchange?

options.text: It makes the exchange largely one-way for as long as the chat is outrunning the reader
It lets the streamer answer every message, since a fast panel means fast replies
options.misconception: reads the speed of the panel as evidence that each message will be answered

options.text: It removes the audience from the exchange, since a livestream has no viewers at all
options.misconception: supposes a live audience to be optional when the whole form depends on one

options.text: It moves the exchange into the recording, so that the live part is only the opening
options.misconception: relocates the conversation to a recording, which is the opposite of what is live

questions.explanation: A livestream has two halves that run at different speeds: one voice producing about a hundred and fifty words a minute, and a panel producing several hundred messages in the same time. When the panel is ahead, the exchange is a broadcast with a response, and a viewer watching later finds the conversation that matters took place off screen. The trap is to read the volume of the chat as participation. What matters is how much of it the streamer could possibly have read.
questions.hint: Ask how many of the messages on the panel could be spoken aloud in the time available.

questions.topic: The conventions of a podcast episode
questions.learningObjective: say what the closing formula of an episode signals
questions.stem: A podcast episode opens with music, the presenter names the topic, two guests talk for an hour, and it ends with a short thanks. What is the thanks at the end doing?

options.text: Signalling the end of the run, so a listener knows nothing more is coming that day
Allowing the speakers to be informal, which they have not been permitted to be before
options.misconception: mistakes a structural marker for a change of register

options.text: Replacing the credits, since an audio episode has no need to name anybody
options.misconception: believes an audio episode has no credits to give at all

options.text: Asking listeners to send material for the next episode, which is its usual purpose
options.misconception: reads the end of a run as a request for contributions

The trap is looking for a purpose in the formula, since a marker works precisely by not doing anything except be recognised.

questions.topic: The constraint behind a broken-up call
questions.learningObjective: name the limit that two-way sound runs into
questions.stem: A video call breaks up exactly when both speakers talk at once. Which constraint is being reached?

options.text: The delay between one side's voice and the other's, which will not carry two at once
The number of people in the room, which the connection divides among all of them
options.misconception: blames the size of the meeting for a fault that appears with two speakers

options.text: The quality of the cameras, which is what a doubled sound signal overloads
options.misconception: points at the pictures when the fault is somewhere in the sound path

options.text: The length of the conversation, which the connection shortens as the call goes on
options.misconception: treats the duration of a call as the cause of a fault that appears within seconds

The trap is looking for the cause among the things a call obviously contains — the room, the cameras, the hour — rather than in the one thing about it that is unusual, which is that it is both live and two-way.

questions.topic: One component of digital literacy
questions.learningObjective: name the component of digital literacy taught by a given exercise
questions.stem: A school asks pupils to establish who published a page, when, and on what evidence. Which component of digital literacy is being taught?

Retrieval, which is the skill of finding a document that is already known to exist
options.misconception: confuses judging a source with locating one, and the two happen at different moments

options.text: Production, which is the ability to write and publish a document of one's own
options.misconception: reads an assessment of somebody else's page as training in making one's own

options.text: Ethics, which is the question of what it is right to publish and what it is right to copy

The trap is a learner who has found a page and assumes the difficulty is over, when the page has not yet been judged at all.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Why length beats complexity in a password
questions.learningObjective: compare two passwords by the number of attempts they allow
questions.stem: Two passwords are offered: « Bleu7! » and « la-poule-courte-du-matin ». Which is stronger, and on what grounds?

options.text: The second, because each extra character multiplies the number of attempts far faster
The first, because one symbol the attacker cannot guess is worth more than several letters
options.misconception: assumes a single unusual character outweighs several extra letters, which is not how guessing works

options.text: The second, because French spelling gives a wider pool of characters than a plain keyboard
options.misconception: reasons from the alphabet rather than from the number of attempts being tried

options.text: The first, because a short password is easier to type and so less likely to be reused
options.misconception: confuses the length of one password with the habit of reusing it, which is the real danger

questions.explanation: Guessing is arithmetic. Each character multiplies the number of combinations by the size of the pool it comes from, so a long ordinary phrase multiplies a small pool several times over, while a short string with one odd character multiplies it only once. Length is also what a person can actually manage, and a phrase can be remembered and typed correctly, which is what separates it from a short password that gets written on a note beside the screen. The trap is the two passwords of unequal length and the habit that makes length irrelevant anyway.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two a person could reproduce from memory in a year.

questions.topic: The signals of a phishing message

questions.topic: Spotting a fraudulent message

Second, the pressure: how much time is the message giving, since a genuine institution does not need a deadline to make a request legitimate, and a request that must be answered inside an hour is a request designed not to be verified. Third, the ask: what exactly is wanted, because a code, a password or a card number will never be asked for by anyone, and a request for nothing in particular is a request for a click rather than for information. Apply it: the address differs from the bank's by two letters, the message gives twenty-four hours, and it wants the reader to click and confirm. Three failures, and the message is not read further.

questions.explanation: Wording is the wrong place to look, because a fraudulent message can be written in perfect French with perfect politeness, and a genuine one can be curt. What makes the method work is that all three tests are checks on the request rather than on the tone, and each can be carried out by the reader alone. What to watch is the fourth habit that a learner will reach for instead, which is to ring the number printed in the message itself, since that number belongs to the person who wrote it.

questions.topic: Judging an online review

A five-star score is one person's impression compressed into a number, and a number looks like the average of many visits, which is why ratings are trusted more than they deserve. The test of checkability is what separates a useful review from a usable one, and it is the only part of the judgement a reader can carry out before booking. What to watch is the temptation to weigh the length most heavily, which rewards the review that has taken the longest to write rather than the one that reports the most.

questions.topic: Building a password a person will actually keep
questions.learningObjective: give three rules that raise strength and survive contact with people
questions.stem: Explain three rules for choosing passwords that raise the strength of an account and will still be followed in a year, and show how each one is applied.

answer.exemplar: Three rules, chosen for the second property first. First, length, because each character multiplies the number of attempts, so four ordinary words in a row are stronger than one unusual symbol and far stronger than the same symbol alone. The words should be chosen for the person and not for the account — a street, a song, a pet — since a rule that requires a note produces a note, and a note beside the keyboard is the password with a second copy. Second, difference between accounts, and the difference matters only for the accounts that can be reached through the first: the mail and the bank, because a password reused twice turns one leak into an account. Third, a second factor on those two, since it does not depend on the password being remembered at all. What none of the three asks for is a rule about symbols, which is the part that gets abandoned first and the part that adds least.

questions.explanation: Strength and keeping are different properties, and a rule that has only one of them will not survive. A password written on a note is weak however long it is, and a password changed every month is strong for eleven days and then written on a new note. The three rules above are the ones that fail least often, because each asks for something the person can do without a record. What to watch is the impulse to make the rules stricter, since every extra condition is a condition somebody will eventually fail quietly rather than admit to.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three rules a person is most likely to break the first time they are in a hurry.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: How a proverb behaves in ordinary speech
questions.learningObjective: explain what a proverb does that an ordinary sentence does not
questions.stem: Explain what a French proverb does for a speaker that an ordinary sentence of advice does not, and show it with a proverb about a task begun and not finished.

answer.exemplar: What a proverb gives a speaker is compression with authority. « Il faut。对此... » — the proverb about not counting a chick before it has hatched compresses a piece of advice into a rhythm that can be said in a second, and the rhythm is what makes it remembered and quotable, which an ordinary sentence of the same advice is not. That is the second thing a proverb does and the reason it is sometimes annoying — it can end a discussion by asserting that the conclusion was obvious all along. The literal version of the image is available too, and a speaker who needs to be understood rather than agreed with is better off explaining.

questions.explanation: The test of what a proverb is for is what happens after it has been said. If the listener is moved to act, the proverb has done its work, and it has done it without an argument being built. If the listener is silenced, the proverb has been used as a door, and that is worth knowing about, because proverbs are available to people who have no argument. What to watch is the borrowed proverb, since a saying imported from another language often does not carry its meaning across and is then used for the shape rather than the sense.
questions.hint: Ask what a speaker can do after the proverb if the listener still does not agree.

questions.topic: Tracing a claim back to a source
questions.learningObjective: give the steps for finding where a figure came from
questions.stem: Explain the steps you would follow to find out where a figure on a page came from, and show what each step produces on a claim that « 62 % des élèves interrogés utilisent un écran le soir », with no source named.

answer.exemplar: Four steps. Read the claim exactly, because most misfires are in the wording rather than the number: who was asked, when, and how many. Then follow the attribution, which on this page is absent, and that absence is the first finding. Then look for the document that would have to exist for the claim to be true — a survey with a date, a sample and a questionnaire — and search for it by its likely title rather than its number. Then judge what the document would have to be for the figure to survive: an enquiry of thirty children in one class will not support 62 % of anything. What that produces is a verdict that the figure is unverified rather than false, and the two are worth different amounts. A claim with no document behind it is not refuted by having no document; it is simply unsourced, and the right response is to leave it alone.

questions.explanation: The steps exist because the work is slow and the temptation is not to do it, and every shortcut lands on a judgement about the page rather than about the number. The largest single gain is usually the second step, since most figures circulate without their method and the absence is visible in seconds. What to watch is the last step, where a careful reader concludes that the figure is false because no document could support it, which is a stronger claim than the evidence allows.
questions.hint: Ask what document would have to exist for the figure to be worth repeating.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the first question asks where the number came from — where does this figure come from, and who measured it? — because a figure with no origin is not a claim anybody can check. The second asks what it is a percentage of, since a rise of forty per cent means nothing until the base, the period and the group are named, and a percentage of what is the whole question. Stage two: if the source is the post, the number was produced by the person asserting it, and no search will turn up an independent version of it. I would not repeat it, and I would not call it false either, because a number invented by its own author is an unverified claim rather than a checked falsehood, and the two are treated very differently by the readers who see them. Calling it false would also credit it with a source it never had.

questions.explanation: Two questions are enough for a first pass, and they are the two that catch the great majority of circulating figures, because most of them have no origin and a great many have no base. The distinction in the second stage matters more than it looks, because a false claim is a thing somebody checked and got wrong, and an unsourced claim is a thing nobody has checked, and telling a reader the first when you have only established the second is its own small dishonesty. What to watch is the urge to explain the mechanism, which is a second question and a different one.
